notes.h: Chapter overview and connections
notes.b: Plate tectonics links the layered structure of Earth to crustal movement. A complete explanation should move from mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull to continental drift and sea-floor spreading, then compare constructive, destructive and conservative boundaries using located examples such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Andes and the San Andreas Fault.

notes.h: Connected course content — Lithospheric plates, Convection currents, Continental drift, Sea-floor spreading
notes.b: These ideas should be used together as part of a process, comparison or case-study explanation. Lithospheric plates: Large rigid sections of the Earth's crust and upper mantle that move and interact at their boundaries, forming plate tectonics. Convection currents: Circular movements of hot mantle material that rise at mid-ocean ridges and sink at subduction zones, driving plate motion. Continental drift: The historical movement of continents across the Earth's surface, supported by evidence from fossil distributions and coastline matching. Sea-floor spreading: The process by which new oceanic crust is created at mid-ocean ridges as magma rises and older crust moves away.

notes.h: Connected course content — Constructive plate boundary, Destructive plate boundary, Transform (conservative) plate boundary, Subduction zone
notes.b: These ideas should be used together as part of a process, comparison or case-study explanation. Constructive plate boundary: A boundary where two plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and form new oceanic crust, creating mid-ocean ridges. Destructive plate boundary: A boundary where an oceanic plate is pushed beneath a continental plate in a process called subduction, forming deep ocean trenches. Transform (conservative) plate boundary: A boundary where two plates slide past each other horizontally, neither creating nor destroying crust. Subduction zone: An area where a denser oceanic plate descends beneath a lighter continental plate, often creating volcanic activity and earthquakes.

notes.h: Connected course content — Slab pull, Mountain range formation
notes.b: These ideas should be used together as part of a process, comparison or case-study explanation. Slab pull: A mechanism driving plate motion where the weight of dense subducting plates pulls surrounding plate material downward. Mountain range formation: The building of mountain ranges through compression at destructive boundaries or folding at plate margins, with examples including the Andes and Irish mountains.

notes.h: Past-paper application — Describe and explain how humans interact with the rock cycle with reference to one of the following: Quarrying, Mining, Oil/Gas exploitation, Geotherm
notes.b: Question focus: Describe and explain how humans interact with the rock cycle with reference to one of the following: Quarrying, Mining, Oil/Gas exploitation, Geothermal energy production. Model content: Humans interact with the rock cycle through quarrying, and the example examined here is the extraction of limestone at the Irish Cement plant at Platin, Co. Meath. What is being extracted and how it formed. The rock being quarried is Carboniferous limestone. It formed about 340 million years ago when Ireland lay under a warm, shallow tropical sea. The shells and skeletons of marine creatures, made of calcium carbonate, settled on the sea floor and built up in layers, and over millions of years these layers were compacted and cemented into rock. That is the sedimentary stage of the rock cycle, and it is where humans intervene. How the quarrying is carried out. The soil and glacial till lying over the limestone — the overburden — is stripped away with excavators. The quarry is then cut in a series of steps or benches so that the working faces stay stable. Holes are drilled into the rock face and charged with explosives, and the rock is broken by controlled blasting. Dumper trucks carry the broken rock to a crusher, where it is reduced in size and screened into grades. Some of it is sold directly as aggregate for concrete and road-building; the rest is burned with shale in a rotary kiln at about 1,450 °C to produce cement clinker, which is ground and mixed with gypsum to make cement. Why this speeds the rock cycle up. Natural weathering and erosion would remove limestone at a rate of a few millimetres in a thousand years. Quarrying removes millions of tonnes a year, so humans have become a more powerful agent of erosion than nature at these sites. Burning the limestone in the kiln also drives carbon dioxide out of the rock and back into the atmosphere, releasing carbon that the rock cycle had locked away for hundreds of millions of years. notes.h: Past-paper application — Describe and explain destructive plate boundaries.
notes.b: Question focus: Describe and explain destructive plate boundaries. Model content: A destructive (convergent) plate boundary occurs where two plates move towards each other and crust is destroyed. The movement is driven by convection currents in the asthenosphere, assisted by slab pull. There are three types. 1. Oceanic plate meeting continental plate. Oceanic crust is basaltic and dense (about 3.0 g/cm³); continental crust is granitic and lighter (about 2.7 g/cm³). Where the two meet the denser oceanic plate is forced down beneath the continental plate along a subduction zone, descending at an angle of roughly 45° into the mantle. A deep ocean trench marks the line of subduction. As the slab descends it is heated by friction and by the surrounding mantle; water driven out of the slab lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge, and magma is generated. Being less dense than the surrounding rock, this magma rises through the continental crust and erupts at the surface. Because it is silica-rich it is viscous and gas-charged, so eruptions are explosive and build steep composite cones. Meanwhile the sediment scraped off the descending slab is crumpled upwards into fold mountains. The Nazca plate subducting beneath the South American plate has produced the Peru–Chile Trench, the Andes and volcanoes such as Cotopaxi; the same arrangement off the west coast of North America gives the Cascades and Mount St Helens. 2. Oceanic plate meeting oceanic plate. The older, colder and therefore denser of the two plates is subducted. A trench again forms at the line of subduction, and the magma generated above the descending slab rises to build a chain of volcanic islands parallel to the trench — an island arc. questions.prompt: Explain how two processes operating inside the Earth cause lithospheric plates to move.
questions.model: Mantle convection transfers heat as hot material rises and cooler material sinks, dragging plates above it. Ridge push moves elevated young crust away from a mid-ocean ridge under gravity. Slab pull occurs where dense oceanic crust sinks at a subduction zone and pulls the rest of the plate behind it.

questions.prompt: Examine the evidence that supports the theory of plate tectonics.
questions.model: Matching continental margins, linked rock structures and identical fossils across oceans support continental drift. Symmetrical magnetic stripes and the increasing age of ocean crust away from ridges demonstrate sea-floor spreading. Global belts of earthquakes, volcanoes and ocean trenches coincide with mapped plate boundaries.

questions.prompt: Compare the processes and landforms found at constructive and destructive plate boundaries, using named examples.
questions.model: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates diverge, pressure falls and basaltic magma creates new oceanic crust, producing a ridge and Icelandic volcanoes. Along the Andes, the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America, causing a trench, powerful earthquakes and explosive volcanoes. Constructive margins create crust; destructive margins recycle it.

notes.h: Past-paper application — Examine how the landscape is changed when a river adjusts to a change in base level, with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
notes.b: Question focus: Examine how the landscape is changed when a river adjusts to a change in base level, with reference to example(s) that you have studied. Model content: Base level is the lowest point to which a river can erode — normally sea level. When base level falls, the river is given renewed energy and begins to cut down again into its own valley. This is called rejuvenation, and it changes the landscape in several distinctive ways. Why base level changes. It falls when the land rises relative to the sea. Isostatic uplift is the commonest cause: during the last glaciation the weight of ice depressed the crust of northern Ireland and Scandinavia, and when the ice melted about 10,000 years ago the land rebounded. Tectonic uplift along a plate boundary produces the same effect, as does a fall in sea level (eustatic change) when water is locked up in ice sheets. Knickpoints. The river cannot adjust its whole long profile at once. It begins cutting down at its mouth and the steepened section works its way upstream. Where the new, steeper profile meets the old, gentler one, there is a sharp break of slope called a knickpoint, usually marked by rapids or a waterfall. The Salmon Leap on the River Liffey at Leixlip and the waterfalls on the tributaries of the Nore are knickpoints of this kind. River terraces. As the river cuts down into its former floodplain, it leaves the old floodplain stranded as a flat bench above the new channel. Because the river erodes from both banks, matching benches are usually left at the same height on either side — paired terraces. If uplift happens repeatedly, a staircase of terraces at different levels results. Good examples are found along the lower Nore and the Barrow. Incised meanders. notes.h: Past-paper application — Explain the formation of two igneous rocks, with reference to Irish examples.
notes.b: Question focus: Explain the formation of two igneous rocks, with reference to Irish examples. Model content: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and solidifies. Whether the magma cools underground or at the surface determines the size of the crystals and therefore the character of the rock. Granite — an intrusive (plutonic) igneous rock. Granite forms when magma rises from the mantle but does not reach the surface. It is trapped within the crust, where it cools very slowly over millions of years because the surrounding rock insulates it. Slow cooling allows the atoms time to arrange themselves into large crystals, so granite is coarse-grained, with crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica clearly visible to the naked eye. The magma solidifies as a large dome-shaped mass called a batholith. Because it forms at depth, granite is only exposed at the surface after the overlying rock has been removed by millions of years of weathering and erosion — and once the pressure of that overburden is released, the granite expands and cracks, producing the joints along which it is later weathered. Granite is hard and resistant, so it tends to stand out as upland. The Wicklow Mountains are a granite batholith emplaced about 400 million years ago during the Caledonian mountain-building period, and the Mourne Mountains in Co. Down are a younger granite intrusion, about 56 million years old. Granite from Wicklow and from Ballyknockan has been widely used as a building and kerb stone. Basalt — an extrusive (volcanic) igneous rock. Basalt forms when lava reaches the surface and cools in contact with the air or with seawater. Cooling is very rapid — days or weeks rather than millions of years — so there is no time for large crystals to grow, and basalt is fine-grained, dark and dense, with crystals too small to see without a microscope. questions.prompt: Account for the contrasting characteristics of shield and composite volcanoes.
questions.model: Shield volcanoes form from fluid basaltic lava that travels far, creating broad gentle slopes and mainly effusive eruptions. Composite volcanoes contain alternating lava and ash produced by viscous, gas-rich magma at destructive margins. Trapped gases make their eruptions more explosive and their slopes steeper.

questions.prompt: Using a named earthquake, explain why the severity of a tectonic hazard depends on human as well as physical factors.
questions.model: In the 2010 Haiti earthquake, a shallow focus close to densely populated Port-au-Prince caused intense shaking. Poorly reinforced buildings, poverty, weak infrastructure and limited emergency capacity greatly increased deaths and delayed aid. Magnitude mattered, but vulnerability and preparedness converted the event into a major disaster.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two measures used to reduce the impact of volcanic or earthquake hazards.
questions.model: Monitoring seismic activity, gas emissions and ground deformation can identify rising risk and support evacuation, but it cannot predict an exact eruption time. Earthquake-resistant design reduces collapse through flexible frames and base isolation, although retrofitting is costly. Education, drills and land-use zoning make both measures more effective.

notes.h: Past-paper application — Explain the role of temperature in the process of physical/mechanical weathering.
notes.b: Question focus: Explain the role of temperature in the process of physical/mechanical weathering. Model content: Temperature is central to physical (mechanical) weathering because rock and the water inside it both change volume as they heat and cool, and repeated volume change breaks rock apart without altering its chemical composition. Freeze-thaw action (frost shattering) needs a temperature that crosses 0 °C repeatedly. Water enters a joint or crack in the rock by day. At night the temperature falls below freezing and the water turns to ice, expanding by about 9% and exerting pressure of up to 2,100 kg per square centimetre on the walls of the crack. By day the ice melts, the water penetrates deeper, and the cycle repeats. After many cycles angular fragments break away and collect at the foot of the slope as scree. This is why freeze-thaw is most effective in upland and periglacial areas — Carrauntoohil, the Mournes and the high corries of the Alps — where temperatures oscillate around freezing point for much of the year, rather than in areas that stay permanently frozen or permanently warm. Exfoliation (onion weathering) depends on a large daily temperature range. In hot deserts such as the Sahara, surface temperatures may reach 50 °C by day and fall close to 0 °C at night. The outer skin of the rock heats and expands more than the cool interior, and because rock is a poor conductor of heat this sets up stress between the layers. Repeated expansion and contraction causes thin curved sheets to peel away from the surface like the layers of an onion, leaving rounded boulders. Granular disintegration works in the same way but at the scale of individual mineral grains: different minerals in a granite expand by different amounts at the same temperature, so the crystals loosen from one another and the rock crumbles into sand. questions.prompt: Explain the formation of one igneous and one sedimentary rock, linking each process to the rock's characteristics.
questions.model: Granite cools slowly from magma underground, allowing large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica to develop. Limestone forms as calcium-rich shells and skeletons accumulate, compact and cement on a sea floor. questions.prompt: Distinguish between weathering and mass movement, and explain one process of each.
questions.model: Weathering breaks rock down in situ, whereas mass movement transfers material downslope under gravity. Freeze-thaw weathering widens cracks when repeated freezing expands water. Soil creep is the very slow downslope movement produced by repeated expansion and contraction, shown by tilted posts and terracettes.

questions.prompt: Account for the development of a limestone pavement and associated underground drainage.
questions.model: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which dissolves calcium carbonate along joints and bedding planes. Enlarged joints become grikes while resistant blocks remain as clints. Continued solution forms swallow holes, caves and passages; calcite deposited from dripping water creates stalactites and stalagmites.

notes.h: Chapter overview and connections
notes.b: Glacial landscapes reflect erosion, transport and deposition by moving ice. Trace how plucking and abrasion create erosional features, how till is transported and deposited, and how landforms such as corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys, drumlins and eskers provide evidence of former glaciation; link isostatic adjustment to crustal recovery after melting.

notes.h: Connected course content — Glaciation, Glacier, Glacial erosion, Glacial deposition
notes.b: These ideas should be used together as part of a process, comparison or case-study explanation. Glaciation: The process of glacier formation and expansion during cold climatic periods, with ice sheets covering large land areas. Glacier: A permanent mass of ice formed from accumulated and compressed snow, moving under gravity in response to temperature and pressure. Glacial erosion: The wearing away of landscape by glaciers through abrasion and plucking, creating distinctive landforms including U-shaped valleys and cirques. Glacial deposition: The laying down of sediment from glacial meltwater and direct ice release, forming features like moraines, drumlins, and outwash plains.

Glacial landforms: Distinctive topographical features created by glacier action, including U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, and fjords. Moraines: Ridges and deposits of sediment left by glaciers, including terminal moraines marking glacier limits and lateral moraines along valley sides. Drumlins: Streamlined hills formed by glacial deposits, elongated in the direction of ice flow, particularly common in Ireland. Isostasy: The vertical movement of the Earth's crust in response to changes in ice mass; land subsides under ice and rebounds after ice melt.

notes.h: Past-paper application — Explain how different rock types produce distinctive landscapes in Ireland, with reference to examples that you have studied.
notes.b: Question focus: Explain how different rock types produce distinctive landscapes in Ireland, with reference to examples that you have studied. Model content: Different rock types weather and erode at different rates and in different ways, and each produces a landscape of its own. Three Irish examples show this clearly. Limestone — the Burren, Co. Clare. Carboniferous limestone is made of calcium carbonate and is permeable, not because the rock itself is porous but because it is cut by horizontal bedding planes and vertical joints. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide to form a weak carbonic acid, which reacts with the calcium carbonate and dissolves it — the process of carbonation. Because the water travels along the joints and bedding planes, the weathering is concentrated there, and a very distinctive landscape results. On the surface, the joints are widened into deep clefts called grikes, leaving flat-topped blocks called clints between them: the limestone pavement of the Burren. Rainwater sinking through the surface enlarges the joints into swallow holes, and underground it dissolves out caves and caverns such as the Aillwee caves, in which redeposited calcite forms stalactites, stalagmites and pillars. Because water disappears underground almost immediately, there are almost no surface streams, and where the water table rises seasonally the hollows fill to form turloughs. The soil cover is thin and the ground bare and grey — the Burren looks like nowhere else in Ireland, and the reason is entirely its rock type. Granite — the Wicklow Mountains. Granite is an intrusive igneous rock formed when magma cooled slowly at depth, giving it large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica. It is hard, impermeable and highly resistant to erosion, so it stands out as upland: the Wicklow Mountains are a batholith emplaced about 400 million years ago and exposed only after the overlying rock was stripped away. questions.prompt: Explain how a corrie develops and show how it may contribute to the formation of an arête.
questions.model: Snow accumulates in a hollow, compacts into ice and moves by rotational slip. Plucking steepens the back wall while abrasion deepens the basin, leaving a rock lip and often a tarn after melting. Model content: Humans interact with the rock cycle through mining operations that extract mineral resources, fundamentally disrupting natural rock formation and cycling processes. Mining represents a major human-rock cycle interaction where bedrock is excavated directly from the Earth to extract valuable minerals including copper, iron, tin and rare earth elements. In open-pit mining operations (such as the Kennecott Bingham Canyon copper mine in Utah), massive volumes of rock are removed, exposing deep crustal material and disrupting overlying rock sequences. This extraction removes rock that would naturally remain part of the endogenic rock cycle (underground at depth or in mountain-building processes). The extracted ore undergoes processing (crushing, smelting, refining) which further processes the rock material through heating and chemical treatment—essentially creating artificial rock metamorphism. Mining generates enormous waste rock piles (overburden) that remain unintegrated in the natural rock cycle. These waste rock piles can occupy areas of hundreds of square kilometres and persist for centuries as non-equilibrium landscape features. The extraction permanently removes rock masses from their original formation process, preventing them from participating in exogenic weathering that would naturally produce sediment. Mining in Ireland, including historical slate mining in Waterford and copper mining in Cork, left permanent voids, subsidence zones and altered topography. Model content: Folding is the structural bending of rock layers in response to compressional stress, typically at convergent plate boundaries, and exerts a primary influence on landform development by creating distinctive ridge-and-valley topography. These fold structures fundamentally influence landscape development. Anticlines, where rock layers arch upward, create ridge landforms because older, more resistant rocks from deeper crustal levels are brought to the surface at the crest of the fold, where they form natural high points resistant to erosion. The Jura Mountains of France and Switzerland exemplify folded landscapes where alternating anticlines (ridges) and synclines (valleys) create dramatic ridge-and-valley morphology extending for hundreds of kilometres in parallel lines. The orientation of folds controls valley and ridge direction—valleys develop along synclines and between anticlines following the fold axis. Folding also influences drainage development. Rivers cut transverse valleys across folded structures where they establish flow before the folds fully develop, creating dramatic gorge passages. notes.b: Question focus: Describe and account for the characteristics of one global climate type that you have studied. Model content: The global climate type described here is the Equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate. CHARACTERISTICS Location. The equatorial climate occupies a belt roughly 5° north and south of the equator, extending to about 10° in places. Its main areas are the Amazon Basin of Brazil, the Congo Basin of central Africa, and the islands of South-East Asia — Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea — together with the west African coast from Guinea to Cameroon. Temperature. Temperatures are uniformly high and remarkably constant. The mean monthly temperature is about 26–28 °C in every month, and the annual range — the difference between the warmest and coolest month — is only 2–3 °C. Manaus, in the Amazon, ranges from about 26 °C to 28 °C across the year. The diurnal range, the difference between day and night, is actually greater than the annual range, at around 8–10 °C, which is why the equatorial night has been called 'the tropics' winter'. There is no seasonal variation of the kind experienced in temperate latitudes. Precipitation. Rainfall is heavy and occurs throughout the year, typically 1,500–3,000 mm annually, with every month receiving over 60 mm. There is no dry season. Rainfall is convectional and follows a marked daily rhythm: mornings are clear and hot, cumulus clouds build through the middle of the day, and heavy thunderstorms with torrential rain occur in the mid to late afternoon, often accompanied by lightning. Relative humidity is very high, typically 80% or more, and the combination of high temperature and high humidity makes the climate feel oppressive. Wind and pressure. Winds are light and variable. notes.h: Past-paper application — Examine how solar energy is transformed and redistributed through circulation patterns in the atmosphere and oceans.
notes.b: Question focus: Examine how solar energy is transformed and redistributed through circulation patterns in the atmosphere and oceans. Model content: SOLAR ENERGY TRANSFORMATION AND REDISTRIBUTION IN ATMOSPHERE AND OCEANS Earth receives approximately 1,361 W/m² solar radiation at top of atmosphere (solar constant). This enormous energy is unevenly distributed geographically and seasonally; atmosphere and oceans redistribute this energy through circulation patterns, creating climate zones and moderating global temperatures. SOLAR ENERGY RECEIPT AND ATMOSPHERIC TRANSFORMATION: Atmospheric Interception: Of incoming solar radiation, approximately 30% is reflected/scattered back to space (albedo effect) by atmosphere, clouds, and surface. Atmospheric gases (particularly water vapor, aerosols) scatter radiation, reducing surface receipt. This atmospheric filtering is essential—without it, surface would receive lethal UV radiation. Radiation Absorption: Atmospheric gases (O₃, N₂O, CO₂, H₂O) absorb radiation at specific wavelengths. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation (protecting life). Water vapor and CO₂ absorb infrared radiation (heat). This selective absorption transforms radiation character—solar radiation penetrates atmosphere relatively easily (visible wavelengths), while terrestrial radiation (infrared) is trapped, creating greenhouse effect. Latitudinal Variation: Solar energy receipt varies with latitude. Equatorial regions receive more intense, year-round solar radiation (sun is nearly overhead). Polar regions receive much less (sun at low angles, seasonal variation extreme—6 months darkness). This creates fundamental temperature gradient driving atmospheric circulation. SEASONAL VARIATION: Earth's axial tilt creates seasonal variation. Northern Hemisphere summer (June) receives maximum solar radiation; winter (December) receives minimum. This 23.5° tilt explains seasonal temperature variation and monsoon patterns

questions.prompt: Explain how the global circulation of the atmosphere redistributes heat and creates major pressure belts.
questions.model: Strong equatorial heating causes air to rise at the ITCZ, cool and produce convectional rain. Air descends near 30 degrees to form subtropical highs and returns as trade winds; mid-latitude westerlies and polar circulation complete the pattern. Earth's rotation deflects winds, while seasonal movement shifts the belts.

questions.prompt: Account for the influence of one ocean current on the climate of adjacent land.
questions.model: The North Atlantic Drift transfers warm water towards western Europe. Prevailing westerlies gain heat and moisture above it, giving Ireland milder winters and a smaller annual temperature range than places at similar latitude. Ocean-atmosphere variability can alter this influence, so the current operates within a wider circulation system.

questions.prompt: Assess how human activity is changing the atmosphere-ocean system.
questions.model: Greenhouse-gas emissions increase retained energy, warming air and oceans, melting land ice and raising sea level through thermal expansion. Oceans absorb carbon dioxide, causing acidification that threatens calcifying organisms. Mitigation reduces emissions while adaptation manages unavoidable impacts; neither is sufficient alone because the system responds over long timescales.

Model content: STRATEGIES FOR MINORITY LANGUAGE SURVIVAL Approximately 3,000-4,000 languages are endangered globally; roughly 90% of world's 7,000+ languages face extinction within two centuries. Minority languages—spoken by populations lacking political power or geographic territory—face particular extinction risk. However, strategies implemented successfully in some regions demonstrate languages can be maintained and revitalized. LANGUAGE ENDANGERMENT CONTEXT: Minority languages face pressures from dominant regional/national languages. Globalization, education systems, media, and economic opportunities favor dominant languages (English, Mandarin, Spanish). Young people often abandon minority languages to access better opportunities, causing intergenerational language loss. Once speakers become bilingual but cease using minority language at home, language erosion accelerates rapidly—third generation often loses minority language entirely. This discrepancy creates tensions, minority rights issues, and challenges to nation-state stability. questions.prompt: Explain how language and religion can both unite and divide a population.
questions.model: A shared language or religion can support belonging, institutions and political mobilisation. Where groups attach competing claims to territory or state power, the same markers may produce exclusion or conflict. Multilingual federalism in Switzerland shows that power-sharing, rights and institutions can accommodate difference rather than making division inevitable.

questions.prompt: Examine how migration and globalisation reshape cultural identity in a named place.
questions.model: Migration introduces languages, food, religion and transnational family links, while global media and brands circulate shared cultural forms. In cities this may create hybrid identities and new cultural economies, but also debates over integration and belonging. Identity is negotiated by migrants and host communities rather than simply replaced by a uniform global culture.

questions.prompt: Assess the role of political boundaries in shaping national or ethnic identity.
questions.model: Borders define citizenship, law and political membership and can strengthen a national story through institutions and education. They may also divide an ethnic group or contain several identities, creating minority-rights questions. Open borders and devolved power can soften effects, while conflict and securitisation make the boundary more socially significant.

notes.h: Past-paper application — Explain how soil characteristics impact on soil development.
notes.b: Question focus: Explain how soil characteristics impact on soil development. Model content: SOIL CHARACTERISTICS AND SOIL DEVELOPMENT: COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS Soil development—the process by which unconsolidated rock material is transformed into soil—is fundamentally shaped by soil characteristics and the environmental factors that influence them. Soil characteristics include colour, texture, structure, organic matter content, pH, and nutrient composition; these interact with climate, parent material, topography, organisms, and time to determine soil development rates and final soil type. SOIL TEXTURE AND DEVELOPMENT: Texture—the proportion of sand, silt, and clay particles—profoundly impacts soil development. Clay-rich soils (high proportion of clay particles) undergo more rapid chemical weathering than sandy soils. Clays retain water due to small particle size and high surface area; water availability accelerates chemical weathering, soil development, and nutrient cycling. However, clay-rich soils develop more slowly than silty soils in terms of structural development (clay particles bind tightly, making drainage poor and workability difficult). Sandy soils develop quickly in terms of drainage and aeration but experience rapid nutrient leaching—downward water movement removes soluble nutrients, limiting soil fertility development. Optimal development occurs in loamy soils (balanced sand-silt-clay ratios): adequate water retention and aeration balance, moderate weathering rates, and good nutrient retention. The parent material determines initial texture. Granite weathering produces sandy soils (quartz dominates). Clay-rich shales produce clay soils. This initial texture cascades through development, influencing all subsequent processes. notes.h: Past-paper application — Discuss how human activity can have both positive and negative impacts on soil.
notes.b: Question focus: Discuss how human activity can have both positive and negative impacts on soil. Model content: HUMAN ACTIVITY IMPACTS ON SOIL: POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE DIMENSIONS Human activities profoundly alter soils, producing complex mixtures of positive and negative impacts. These impacts range from soil conservation and improvement to severe degradation threatening food security and ecosystem function. The net outcome depends on management approach and context. NEGATIVE IMPACTS—SOIL DEGRADATION: Soil Erosion from Agriculture: Tilling (ploughing) disrupts soil structure, exposing soil particles to wind and water erosion. Removing vegetation cover eliminates root systems stabilizing soil; rain impacts directly on exposed soil, detaching particles; water runoff concentrates and causes gullying. Intensive agriculture combines these factors: monoculture (single crop) leaves soil bare between plantings; ploughing increases erodibility. Global erosion rates from agriculture are approximately 24 billion tons annually—far exceeding natural soil formation rates (~1 ton/hectare/year). This causes: topsoil loss (nutrient-rich layer disappears), reduced fertility, increased sediment in waterways (water pollution), and desertification (severe erosion creating wastelands). Irish Example: Hillside erosion in upland farming areas (sheep grazing on steep slopes) causes gullying and surface runoff, degrading soil productivity. Compaction: Heavy machinery (tractors, combines) compresses soil, destroying structure and reducing porosity. Compacted soils experience: poor drainage (waterlogging, anaerobic conditions), reduced aeration (root growth restricted), and declined biological activity (organisms suffocate in oxygen-poor conditions). questions.prompt: Explain how climate, organisms and parent material interact in the formation of a named soil.
questions.model: In a brown earth, moderate rainfall permits some leaching without removing all bases, while deciduous litter decomposes rapidly to form mull humus. Soil organisms mix organic and mineral material, and permeable parent material supports drainage. These interactions produce a moderately fertile profile with less distinct horizons than a podzol.

questions.prompt: Account for two plant adaptations found in a named biome.
questions.model: In tropical rainforest, drip-tip leaves shed intense rainfall and reduce fungal growth, while buttress roots support tall trees in shallow nutrient-rich surface layers. Evergreen leaves allow continuous photosynthesis in year-round warmth. Each adaptation responds to climate, competition or the rapid nutrient cycle rather than being an isolated feature.

questions.prompt: Assess the effects of one human activity on nutrient cycling and sustainability in a biome.
questions.model: Rainforest clearance removes the biomass that stores most nutrients and breaks rapid recycling through litter. Exposed soil is leached and eroded, so short-lived farm yields may be followed by declining fertility, biodiversity loss and carbon emissions. Agroforestry, selective logging and protected areas can retain more cycling, but require enforcement and viable livelihoods.

notes.b: Question focus: We live in an interdependent global economy. Actions or decisions taken in one area have an impact on other areas. Discuss this statement with reference to desertification and deforestation. Model content: The statement is that we live in an interdependent global economy, and that actions taken in one place affect others. Desertification and deforestation both demonstrate this: each has local causes rooted in global demand, and each has consequences that cross national borders and reach people who had no part in causing them. DESERTIFICATION What it is and where. Desertification is the degradation of dryland into desert-like conditions. The clearest example is the Sahel, the semi-arid belt running from Senegal through Mali, Niger and Chad to Sudan, where the Sahara has advanced southwards and productive land has been lost across an area larger than western Europe. The UN estimates that around 12 million hectares of productive land are lost worldwide each year. Local causes, global drivers. The immediate causes are overgrazing, overcultivation, deforestation for fuelwood and poor irrigation. But the decisions behind them are shaped elsewhere. Cash cropping for export — cotton in Mali and Burkina Faso, groundnuts in Senegal — was introduced under colonial rule and is sustained by world commodity markets; it occupies the best land and pushes subsistence farmers onto marginal soils. When world prices fall, farmers must plant more to earn the same, so degradation accelerates. Structural adjustment programmes imposed by the IMF and World Bank in the 1980s required governments to cut agricultural subsidies and expand exports, with the same effect. Meanwhile agricultural subsidies in the EU and United States depress world prices for the crops Sahelian farmers sell, so a policy decision taken in Brussels or Washington directly reduces the income of a farmer in Niger and pushes them to overwork their land. notes.b: Question focus: Sustainability is a model for future human and economic development. Discuss this statement with reference to three of the following: Resource use, Fair trade, Justice issues, Self-reliance. Model content: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — the definition given in the Brundtland Report of 1987. Three aspects are discussed here: resource use, fair trade, and self-reliance. RESOURCE USE The problem. The world's economy is built on resources consumed far faster than they are replaced. Fossil fuels took hundreds of millions of years to form and are being burned in a few centuries; groundwater in the Punjab and the American High Plains is being pumped out faster than it recharges; fish stocks have been reduced to a fraction of their former size; and soil is eroded faster than it forms. Consumption is also grossly unequal: if everyone lived as the average person in Ireland or the United States does, humanity would need several planets. Renewable resources become non-renewable in practice once they are used beyond their rate of replacement. Sustainable practice. Sustainability requires using renewable resources within their replacement rate and substituting renewables for finite ones. questions.prompt: Explain how unequal terms of trade can reinforce dependency in a developing country.
questions.model: A country dependent on a few primary exports faces volatile and often low prices while importing higher-value manufactured goods. Falling export revenue reduces funds for infrastructure, health and diversification and may increase borrowing. Processing commodities locally, regional trade and fairer market access can retain more value, though each needs skills and investment.

questions.prompt: Evaluate one top-down and one bottom-up strategy for development.
questions.model: A large dam can supply electricity, irrigation and national infrastructure but may displace communities, damage ecosystems and concentrate benefits. A community-led water, credit or farming project uses local knowledge and can build ownership, though its scale and finance are limited. Effective development often connects accountable national investment with genuine local participation.

questions.prompt: Assess the claim that trade is more effective than aid in reducing global inequality.
questions.model: Trade can create continuing income, employment and productive capacity, but benefits depend on market access, prices, domestic linkages and labour standards. Aid can fund health, education and emergency needs that markets neglect, yet may be tied or donor-driven. The strongest judgement considers fair trade rules, capable institutions and targeted aid as complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
